NFL Key Numbers Beyond 3 and 7: Why 10, 14, and 17 Also Shape the Spread Market

Published November 4, 2026 · 10 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Ask a bettor to name an NFL key number and you'll hear "3" before the question is even finished, with "7" close behind. That's fair — those two numbers do more work in the spread market than any others. But treating them as the entire key-number conversation misses a second tier that still moves real money: 10, 14, 6, 4, and 17 each show up often enough in final margins that sportsbooks price around them too, and bettors who only know about the field goal and the touchdown are leaving value on the table when it comes to buying points, building teasers, or just reading why a line sits where it does.

In this guide

  1. What "key number" actually means
  2. The full ranking, not just the top two
  3. 10: two scores in one number
  4. 14 and 6: the next tier down

What "key number" actually means

A key number is simply a final-margin value that NFL games land on far more often than random chance would predict. If scoring margins were evenly spread across every possible integer, a sportsbook could price a half-point move anywhere on the board the same way. They don't, because football scoring isn't random — it's built out of 3-point field goals, 6-point touchdowns, and 7- or 8-point touchdowns with the extra point or two-point try attached, plus the occasional safety. Add two of those scoring events together across a 60-minute game and certain sums simply come up more often than others. Our guide to the .5 hook at 3 and 7 covers why those two specific numbers get the half-point treatment; this one zooms out to the rest of the list.

The short version: a key number isn't a superstition — it's a byproduct of how football is scored. The further a number sits from a plausible combination of 3s, 6s, and 7s, the less often games actually finish on it, and the less a sportsbook needs to defend it with extra pricing.

The full ranking, not just the top two

Decades of final-score data compiled by betting analysts consistently puts 3 at the top of the list by a wide margin, 7 second, and then a cluster of secondary numbers in roughly this order: 6, 10, 4, 14, and 17, with everything else trailing well behind and flattening out into something closer to noise. The exact ranking shifts slightly depending on the sample of seasons used, but the shape of the curve doesn't — there's a steep cliff after 3 and 7, a smaller but still meaningful bump at 6, 10, and 14, and then a long, flat tail.

MarginWhy it comes upRelative frequency tier
3One field goal; the single most common margin in footballHighest
7One touchdown with the extra pointVery high
6One touchdown with a missed extra point, or a converted two-point try minus one score elsewhereElevated
10A field goal plus a touchdown (3 + 7)Elevated
4A field goal plus a missed extra point, or a late safety changing a 7-point gameModerate
14Two touchdowns with both extra points (7 + 7)Moderate
17Two touchdowns plus a field goal (7 + 7 + 3)Mild

Notice the pattern: every number on this list is built from the same three building blocks — 3, 6, and 7 — stacked in different combinations. That's not a coincidence, it's the entire explanation for why key numbers exist at all.

10: two scores in one number

Ten is arguably the most underrated key number in football, because it's the simplest possible combination you can build once a game has more than one scoring play: a field goal and a touchdown. A huge share of NFL games end with one team winning by exactly a field goal-plus-touchdown margin — think a 24-14 final, or a 27-17 one — which makes 10 the third most common final margin in most historical breakdowns, trailing only 3 and 7. A spread of pick'em to 3 crosses one key number; a spread that moves from 7 to 10, or 10 to 13, is crossing one of the next tier down, and sportsbooks price that move accordingly rather than treating every half-point increment as equally cheap.

14 and 6: the next tier down

Fourteen is the two-touchdown version of 7 — exactly double it — and shows up constantly in games where one team simply scores twice as many touchdowns as the other with both extra points good. It's common enough that a two-touchdown favorite's spread sitting at 13.5 instead of 14.5 is a deliberate half-point of protection for the book, not an accident.

Six is a little less intuitive. It mostly comes from a touchdown with a missed or blocked extra point, which isn't an everyday event, but it also shows up any time the arithmetic of multiple scores nets out to a 6-point gap — a field goal and a field goal and a missed two-point try, for instance, or a safety shaving a point off what would otherwise have been a 7-point game. Because there's more than one way to arrive at 6, it ends up more common than you'd expect for a number built on a "miss," and it sits solidly in the second tier alongside 10.

17 and 4: smaller, but not nothing

Seventeen is two touchdowns plus a field goal — the natural next step up from 10 and 14 — and it comes up often enough that a line parked at 16.5 rather than 17.5 is, again, not arbitrary. Four is the mirror image of 10: instead of a made field goal plus a touchdown, it's a missed extra point layered onto a field-goal margin, or a late safety nudging a 7-point final down to 4. Both numbers matter enough to earn a half-point of cushion in a well-priced market, even though neither comes close to the gravitational pull of 3 or 7.

Where the list stops mattering: once you get past 17, the "which combination of 3s, 6s, and 7s gets you here" exercise runs out of common paths, and frequency drops off fast. Margins like 1, 2, 5, 9, 11, 13, 15, 16, and almost everything north of 17 behave close to randomly — which is exactly why books don't bother defending them with extra half-points the way they do the numbers above.

How this changes the price of buying a point

Buying a half-point or full point off a spread costs more when that move crosses a meaningful key number, and less when it doesn't — and "meaningful" extends well past 3 and 7. Moving a favorite from -3.5 to -3 crosses the single most expensive number in football, so books charge a premium for it. Moving from -10.5 to -10, or -14.5 to -14, crosses a second-tier number and typically costs a bit more than a routine half-point move, even if it's cheaper than crossing 3. Moving from -8.5 to -8, by contrast, crosses almost nothing of statistical significance, so that buy tends to be priced close to a standard increment. Our guide to alternate spreads goes deeper on how books build the full menu of lines around a game; the key-number map above is the reason that menu isn't priced in even steps.

This same logic is the backbone of the Wong teaser, which is built specifically around crossing both 3 and 7 on each leg. A teaser or points-buy strategy built only around 10 or 14 instead can still make sense, but it's working with meaningfully less edge than one that crosses the two biggest numbers on the board, and recognizing that gap before you build a ticket is the difference between a strategy with real backing and one that just feels clever.

Reading a line with the full map in mind

The practical payoff of knowing this full list isn't a betting system — it's a better read on why a given line looks the way it does. When you see a spread sitting at an odd-looking number like 6.5 or 10.5 instead of a round number, it's rarely random; it usually means the book is parking the line just on the expensive side of a key number rather than directly on it, so a bettor can't buy through it for free. Once you can spot the full set of numbers — not just 3 and 7, but 6, 10, 14, 4, and 17 — the pricing of alternate lines, teasers, and points-buy menus stops looking arbitrary and starts looking like exactly what it is: a market built around how football actually gets scored.

Frequently asked questions

Is 10 really more common than people think as a final NFL margin?

Yes — most historical breakdowns of NFL final margins put 10 in third place behind only 3 and 7, since it's simply the sum of the two most common scoring plays in football: one field goal and one touchdown.

Do sportsbooks put a half-point hook on every key number, or just 3 and 7?

Books are most consistent about hooking 3 and 7 because those numbers carry the most weight, but it's common to see half-point hooks at 10 and 14 as well, especially on games where the market expects a comfortable favorite. Smaller key numbers like 4, 6, and 17 get hooked less consistently and mostly on games where the number sits close to the expected margin.

Why does 6 show up more than a number like 5 or 9?

Six has multiple realistic paths to it — a missed extra point after a touchdown, or a safety trimming a point off a 7-point game — while 5 and 9 don't correspond cleanly to any common combination of 3-point and 6- or 7-point scores, so they come up closer to randomly.

Does this key-number list apply the same way to college football?

The same underlying logic applies, since college football is scored with the same building blocks, but the distribution is flatter because college games include far more blowouts and extra-point-adjacent quirks like two-point conversions after a targeting ejection. Our college football spreads guide gets into why the shape of the margin curve differs from the NFL's.

Should I build a teaser around 10 and 14 instead of 3 and 7?

You can, and it isn't a bad bet by itself, but it's working with less statistical backing than a teaser built around 3 and 7, since those two numbers carry far more of the total frequency than 10 and 14 combined. Treat a 10/14 teaser as a secondary option, not a direct substitute.
